text: react-virtualized is a collection of React components for efficiently rendering large lists and tabular data. Only the rows and columns visible within the viewport are rendered, which keeps the number of DOM elements small no matter how much data there is. If you're starting a new project, also take a look at react-window as a lighter-weight alternative. Installation Begin by installing the library from NPM: npm install react-virtualized TypeScript definitions are included within the published dist folder. text: CellMeasurer is a higher-order component that automatically measures a cell's contents just-in-time, e.g. for messages in a chat interface whose size isn't known until they've been rendered. Specify a fixed width to measure dynamic height (or vice versa). CellMeasurer can be used with Grid, List, Table, MultiGrid, and Masonry. If sizes can be determined ahead of time (e.g. from the data), it's simpler and more efficient to pass a rowHeight or columnWidth function than to measure cells; see variable row heights and variable sizes. Use CellMeasurer when a cell's size depends on its rendered content (e.g. wrapping text or images). This is an advanced component, with some limitations and performance considerations; see limitations and performance.

text: Measuring a column's width requires measuring all of the rows in order to determine the widest occurrence of that column. The same is true in reverse for measuring a row's height. For this reason it may not be a good idea to use CellMeasurer for Grids containing a large number of both columns and rows. (This is also why a CellMeasurerCache should be configured with either fixedWidth or fixedHeight.) Since cells are measured one at a time as they are rendered, performance can suffer if a user skips many rows (or columns) at once, by dragging the scrollbar or by calling a method like scrollToCell or scrollToRow. There is (unfortunately) no workaround for this limitation at the moment. If sizes can be determined ahead of time (e.g. from the data), it's more efficient to pass a rowHeight or columnWidth function than to measure cells.

headings.title: How do I upgrade from version 9?
headings.text: How do I upgrade from version 9? Version 10 requires React 18 or newer, removes a few components (AutoSizer, Collection and WindowScroller), and replaces the controlled scroll props (e.g. scrollToIndex) with methods. The migration guide in the changelog covers each change, with before/after examples.

headings.title: Why is nothing rendered (or why does AutoSizer report a height of 0)?
headings.text: Why is nothing rendered (or why does AutoSizer report a height of 0)? List, Grid, Table, and Masonry need an explicit height and width (only a width when they are scrolled by the window). AutoSizer (from the react-virtualized-auto-sizer package) can provide them, but it only fills its parent; it won't stretch it. If the parent (or one of its ancestors) has no height, AutoSizer reports 0 and nothing is rendered. Give the parent a size (e.g. height: 100% or flex: 1); inside a flex container, wrap AutoSizer in a div with flex: 1 1 auto. See sizing components for more.

headings.title: How do I scroll to a row (or cell)?
headings.text: How do I scroll to a row (or cell)? Call scrollToRow({ index, align }) on a List or Table, or scrollToCell({ columnIndex, rowIndex, align }) on a Grid, through a ref. In version 10, these methods replace the scrollToIndex and scrollToRow props. They scroll once: the row isn't kept in view if sizes change afterwards, so to scroll to a row that is being added, call them once it has rendered (e.g. in an effect). To render a list at a scroll position from the start (e.g. when restoring it), use the initialScrollTop prop instead.

headings.title: How do I make a list scroll with the rest of the page?
headings.text: How do I make a list scroll with the rest of the page? Set the scrollElement prop of a List, Grid, Table or Masonry to "window" (or to a scrollable element). The component then renders at its full height, renders only the rows visible within the window, and its scroll methods scroll the window; it only needs a width. In version 10, this replaces WindowScroller. See window scrolling.

headings.title: Why do my Table and other components look unstyled?
headings.text: Why do my Table and other components look unstyled? react-virtualized ships a small set of default styles that must be imported once, e.g. when your application starts: import "react-virtualized/styles.css";. You can also skip them and provide your own; see customizing styles.

headings.title: Why doesn't my list update when my data changes?
headings.text: Why doesn't my list update when my data changes? The components only re-render when their props change (shallow comparison). If your data changes but props like rowCount don't (e.g. after re-sorting), either pass the changed value through as an extra prop (e.g. sortBy={sortBy}) or force an update: forceUpdateGrid() for List and Table, forceUpdate() for Grid and Masonry.

headings.title: My row heights (or column widths) changed. Why is the layout stale?
headings.text: My row heights (or column widths) changed. Why is the layout stale? Sizes are cached once they have been computed, because the components only know rowCount/columnCount and can't tell when the underlying data changes. Call recomputeRowHeights(index) on List or Table, or recomputeGridSize({ columnIndex, rowIndex }) on Grid, starting from the first index whose size changed. (This is only needed when sizes come from a function; changes to a numeric rowHeight or columnWidth are applied automatically.)

headings.title: When should I clear a CellMeasurerCache?
headings.text: When should I clear a CellMeasurerCache? CellMeasurer measures each cell once and caches the result. Call cache.clear(rowIndex, columnIndex) when a cell's content changes (e.g. a loading indicator is replaced with content), and cache.clearAll() when all cells need to reflow (e.g. the width changed and text wraps differently); then tell the parent to recompute its sizes (recomputeRowHeights() on a List or Table, recomputeGridSize() on a Grid). See CellMeasurerCache. If items can be added, removed, or re-ordered, pass a keyMapper (e.g. mapping indices to item IDs) so cached sizes follow the items rather than their indices.

headings.title: Can CellMeasurer measure both widths and heights?
headings.text: Can CellMeasurer measure both widths and heights? Not efficiently: a row's height is the tallest cell in that row (and a column's width is the widest cell in that column), so measuring requires rendering every cell in it. Use fixedWidth or fixedHeight on the CellMeasurerCache to measure only one dimension. Measuring can also be slow when users jump far ahead with the scrollbar, so provide sizes up front when you can.

headings.title: Should I use react-virtualized or react-window?
headings.text: Should I use react-virtualized or react-window? react-window is a smaller, lighter-weight library by the same author, with a simpler API, and is a good choice for new projects that need a list or grid. react-virtualized offers more components (e.g. Table, Masonry, MultiGrid, CellMeasurer, and InfiniteLoader), and version 10 keeps existing applications working on modern React.

headings.text: Choosing a value Overscanning has performance implications: the higher the value, the more cells need to be rendered in reaction to each scroll event. (See this slide for a visual example of how windowing works.) Setting an overscan value too high will erase the performance gains achieved by virtualization. Use the default value (10 rows) as a starting point and lower it if possible; aim for the lowest value that still generally avoids empty space appearing during normal scrolling. The same advice applies to overscanColumnCount. Consider tuning these values when: Cells are expensive to render: lower the overscan count so that less work is done per scroll event (and consider rendering a light-weight placeholder using the isScrolling parameter). Cells are cheap to render but blank space appears while scrolling quickly: raise the overscan count a little. A grid scrolls horizontally: overscanColumnCount defaults to 0, so a small value may help with horizontal scrolling.

headings.text: Measured content CellMeasurer can only measure cells in the browser, so on the server (and during hydration) rows are rendered at the cache's default sizes, and they are re-positioned once they have been measured. Choose default sizes close to the typical size of your content to minimize the shift.

headings.title: Limitations
headings.text: Limitations A component with a scrollElement is rendered from its top on the server, using its height prop as the height of the viewport; once hydrated, it renders the rows visible within the scroll element (e.g. the window). Its vertical position is determined by the scroll element, so initialScrollTop doesn't apply. Masonry doesn't support an initial scroll offset: cell positions are only known once the cells before them have been measured, which can't happen on the server. The scrollbar size is measured after hydration, so the space reserved for scrollbars may change slightly at that point.

text: react-virtualized components can be rendered on the server (e.g. with renderToString or a framework like Next.js) and hydrated on the client. The server renders the rows (or cells) that would be visible, so the page shows content before JavaScript has loaded. This guide covers the things to keep in mind.

headings.title: Filling the available space
Why are width and height undefined?
Why is my AutoSizer setting a height of 0?
headings.text: Why is my AutoSizer setting a height of 0? AutoSizer expands to fill its parent but it will not stretch the parent. If AutoSizer is reporting a height (or width) of 0, then it's likely that the parent element (or one of its parents) has a height of 0. One easy way to test this is to temporarily add a style to the parent (e.g. background-color: red) to check that it is the size you expect. You may need to add height: 100% or flex: 1 to the parent.

headings.title: Can I use AutoSizer to manage only width or height (not both)?

headings.text: Responding to size changes Use the onResize prop to be notified when the size changes, e.g. to clear a CellMeasurer cache when the width changes and text wraps differently. See react-virtualized-auto-sizer for its other props.

headings.title: Migrating from react-virtualized 9.x
headings.text: Migrating from react-virtualized 9.x Earlier versions of react-virtualized included an AutoSizer component. It has been removed in version 10. To migrate to react-virtualized-auto-sizer (version 2): Import AutoSizer from "react-virtualized-auto-sizer" rather than "react-virtualized". Replace the children render function with the renderProp prop (or with the ChildComponent prop; see below). Handle undefined sizes: width and height are undefined until the parent has been measured (including during server rendering). Remove disableHeight and disableWidth; just ignore the dimension that you don't need. Remove defaultHeight and defaultWidth; render a placeholder while the size is undefined instead.

text: Many react-virtualized components (e.g. List, Grid, and Table) require explicit pixel dimensions, but sometimes you just want a component to grow to fill all of the available space. The react-virtualized-auto-sizer package measures its parent element and passes the available width and height to its child. (A component that is scrolled by the window only needs a width; see below.) As of version 10, AutoSizer is no longer part of react-virtualized; use the react-virtualized-auto-sizer package instead. It works with all react-virtualized components (and with react-window). See migrating from react-virtualized 9.x below. npm install react-virtualized-auto-sizer

text: A cell positioner is a function that is given a cell index and returns the cell's position: (index) => ({ left, top }). It is called in index order, once for each cell, after that cell has been measured; so it can read the cell's height (and the heights of all earlier cells) from the CellMeasurerCache. The positions it returns are cached by Masonry.
title: Cell positioners

text: Masonry layouts are often used to display images. Because cell measurements must be synchronous, the size of each image must be known before its cell is rendered (eg by setting an explicit height and width on the , using dimensions provided by the server). Otherwise the cell would be measured before the image loads, and the measurement would be wrong. In the basic example, colored blocks with a known height stand in for images; an image with known dimensions works the same way. Scale the height to the column width to preserve the image's aspect ratio, eg columnWidth * (imageHeight / imageWidth). Items can only be measured once; measurements are cached permanently (until the cache is cleared). If image sizes aren't known up front (eg the server can't provide them), they need to be pre-measured before they are passed to Masonry. To preserve a correct layout, images can only be displayed one by one in the order they appear in the list (not in the order they finish loading). The react-virtualized-image-measurer library handles this; it loads the images, then passes each item along with its size to a render function that renders the Masonry (live demo).
title: Images

headings.title: Layout constraints
headings.text: Layout constraints Multi-column layouts are supported. Each cell can have a unique, lazily-measured height. Cells may not span multiple columns: the width of all cells in a column should be equal (and must not exceed the column's width), and the left position of all cells within a column must align. Cell measurements must be synchronous. A cell's size impacts the layout, and asynchronous measurements would require frequent layout invalidation. The asynchronous measure function passed to CellMeasurer's render callback is not supported by Masonry. (See images for how to handle content such as images whose size isn't known up front.)

headings.title: Animation constraints
headings.text: Animation constraints Simple animations are supported (eg translating or sliding cells into place when they are first revealed). More complex animations are not (eg cells flying from one position to another on resize).

text: Rendering occurs in two phases: Measurement: Estimated cell sizes (the defaultHeight and defaultWidth of the cellMeasurerCache) are used to decide how many cells to measure in a batch. The batch size is chosen using a fast, naive layout algorithm that stacks cells in order until the viewport has been filled. After measurement is complete, Masonry evaluates the positioned cells to determine whether another measurement pass is required (eg if actual cell sizes were smaller than the estimated sizes). All measurements are permanently cached (keyed by keyMapper) for performance purposes. Layout: The external cellPositioner is used to position cells. At this point the positioner has access to cached size measurements for all of the cells it is asked to position. The positions it returns are cached by Masonry for fast access later. The measurement phase is repeated if the user scrolls beyond the bounds of the current layout. If the layout is invalidated (eg due to a resize), cached positions can be cleared using recomputeCellPositions() or clearCellPositions() . By default, measurements and positions are cached by index. If cells can be re-ordered (or inserted), provide a keyMapper that maps an index to a unique id, and use the same mapping for the CellMeasurerCache's keyMapper, so that cached measurements aren't associated with the wrong cells.
title: Measuring and layout

text:
This component efficiently displays arbitrarily positioned cells using windowing techniques.
Cell position is determined by an injected cellPositioner property.
Windowing is vertical; this component does not support horizontal scrolling.
 Rendering occurs in two phases:

First pass uses estimated cell sizes (provided by the cache) to determine how many cells to measure in a batch.
Batch size is chosen using a fast, naive layout algorithm that stacks images in order until the viewport has been filled.
After measurement is complete (once the render has been committed) this component evaluates positioned cells
in order to determine if another measurement pass is required (eg if actual cell sizes were less than estimated sizes).
All measurements are permanently cached (keyed by keyMapper) for performance purposes.
Second pass uses the external cellPositioner to layout cells.
At this time the positioner has access to cached size measurements for all cells.
The positions it returns are cached by Masonry for fast access later.
Phase one is repeated if the user scrolls beyond the current layout's bounds.
If the layout is invalidated due to eg a resize, cached positions can be cleared using recomputeCellPositions().

 Animation constraints:
Simple animations are supported (eg translate/slide into place on initial reveal).
More complex animations are not (eg flying from one position to another on resize).
 Layout constraints:
This component supports multi-column layout.
The height of each item may vary.
The width of each item must not exceed the width of the column it is "in".
The left position of all items within a column must align.
(Items may not span multiple columns.)

children: (params: ScrollSyncChildProps) => ReactNode Function responsible for rendering 2 or more virtualized components.
It is passed the current scroll and size values (clientHeight, clientWidth, scrollHeight, scrollLeft, scrollTop, scrollWidth),
an onScroll callback that should be passed through to the virtualized children that the user can scroll,
and a registerChild function that returns a ref callback for each virtualized child that should be kept in sync

The scroll and size values can also be used for custom rendering (e.g. shading based on the scroll offset).

headings.title: Column sizes
headings.text: Column sizes A column's width is its flex basis. Columns can grow (flexGrow, defaults to 0) to fill unused space, or shrink (flexShrink, defaults to 1) when there is not enough room, within the bounds of minWidth and maxWidth. See the Column props for more.

headings.title: Column components
headings.text: Column components Column doesn't render anything itself: Table reads the props of its children (applying the Column defaults, also exported as defaultColumnProps) to render headers and cells. Falsy children are ignored, so columns can be shown or hidden conditionally. Because the defaults are applied to any child element, a component that wraps Column can be used as a column as well, e.g. const NameColumn = (props: ColumnProps) => <Column {...props} /> rendered as <NameColumn dataKey="name" label="Name" width={120} />. (The wrapper itself is never rendered, so it should only forward or compute props.) In version 10, Column is a function component; subclassing Column (class MyColumn extends Column) is no longer supported. Use a wrapper component instead. Next, learn how to style rows and use dynamic row heights, customize cells and headers or entire rows, or sort a table.

headings.text:
forceUpdateGrid Forcefully re-render the inner Grid component.
Calling forceUpdate on Table may not re-render the inner Grid since it uses shallowCompare as a performance optimization.
Use this method if you want to manually trigger a re-render.
This may be appropriate if the underlying row data has changed but the row sizes themselves have not.

headings.title: recomputeRowHeights
headings.text:
recomputeRowHeights Recompute row heights and offsets after the specified index (defaults to 0).
Table has no way of knowing when its underlying list data has changed since it only receives a rowHeight property.
If the rowHeight is a number it can compare before and after values but if it is a function that comparison is error prone.
In the event that a dynamic rowHeight function is in use and the row heights have changed this function should be manually called by the "smart" container parent.
This method will also force a render cycle (via forceUpdate) to ensure that the updated measurements are reflected in the rendered table.

headings.text:
scrollToPosition Scroll to the specified vertical offset; scrollLeft is ignored (tables don't scroll horizontally).
Offsets are clamped to the scrollable range. This allows a Table to be used with ScrollSync.
Useful for animating position changes.
If the Table has a scrollElement, the scroll element (e.g. the window) is scrolled instead.

headings.title: scrollToRow
headings.text:
scrollToRow Ensure the row at the specified index is visible (scrolling if necessary).
This method can be used to safely scroll back to a row that a user has scrolled away from even if it was previously scrolled to.
The align parameter (default "auto") controls the alignment of the row:
"auto" scrolls the least amount possible to ensure that the specified row is fully visible
(a row taller than the table is aligned to its start, so that its start is visible);
"start" aligns the row to the top of the table and "end" to the bottom; "center" aligns it in the middle.
This is a one-time scroll: the row is not kept in view afterwards (e.g. if the table's size or its row heights change).
Rows that haven't been measured yet (e.g. by CellMeasurer) are positioned using their estimated heights.
If the Table has a scrollElement, the scroll element (e.g. the window) is scrolled instead.
 scrollToRow(params: { align?: Alignment; index: number }): void;

headings.title: SortDirection
headings.text: SortDirection The SortDirection constant specifies which direction data is sorted in: SortDirection.ASC ("ASC") sorts items in ascending order, from the lowest value to the highest (e.g. a-z, 0-9). SortDirection.DESC ("DESC") sorts items in descending order, from the highest value to the lowest (e.g. z-a, 9-0).

headings.title: SortIndicator
Returning to the natural order
headings.text: Returning to the natural order Once a Table has been sorted, the built-in sort directions only toggle between ascending and descending; there is no way to return to the unsorted, “natural” order. The natural sort tables guide shows how to implement this in your application code.

headings.title: Sorting by multiple columns
headings.text: Sorting by multiple columns By default, Table assumes that its data will be sorted by a single attribute. The createTableMultiSort utility can be used to sort by multiple fields; see the multi-column sort tables guide. Sorting large data sets can be expensive; memoize the sorted data (e.g. with useMemo) so that it is only re-sorted when the sort criteria change.
